1) Chronic venous stasis dermatitis with secondary purpura/erosions — Most likely. Fits medial-foot distribution, bilateral edema, burning worse with standing, histology showing dermal fibrosis, extravasated erythrocytes, focal hemosiderin and perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate.  

2) Axitinib-associated acral/hand‑foot drug reaction (palmar‑plantar erythrodysesthesia/pressure‑point toxicity) — Probable contributor. Timing (lesions began ~6 months after starting axitinib), bilateral painful erosions on the feet and epidermal necrosis on biopsy support a drug‑related acral toxicity.  

3) Drug‑induced lymphocytic small‑vessel vasculitis — Possible. Histology with prominent perivascular lymphocytes and lymphocytes within vessel walls, negative DIF and lack of leukocytoclasia/fibrinoid necrosis favors a lymphocytic (rather than leukocytoclastic) vasculitic/drug reaction, which can be medication‑triggered.  

4) Livedoid vasculopathy (atrophie blanche spectrum) — Less likely. Clinical pattern of painful reticulated purpura and erosions overlaps, but classic histologic thrombotic/fibrin changes were not seen and thrombosis workup was unrevealing.  

5) Pressure/contact/friction‑related dermatitis with secondary hemorrhage or superficial infection — Least likely but possible given symptoms worse with standing and interdigital involvement; histology and lack of infectious organisms make primary infection less likely.

Recommended next steps to confirm and manage (brief):
- Duplex venous ultrasound of lower extremities to assess for venous reflux/insufficiency.
- Review axitinib timing/dose with the oncology team — consider dose reduction or temporary hold if drug reaction suspected.
- Local wound care, elevation and compression (if venous insufficiency confirmed and no arterial compromise), topical emollients/low‑potency corticosteroid for inflammation, and analgesia.
- If diagnostic uncertainty persists, consider repeat or deeper biopsy focused on vessel evaluation and/or vascular clinic referral.
